utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present, that is, that Mr. Borovcanin has returned. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic and Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution is represented today by Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Mitchell. All right. The witness is also present in the courtroom. Mr. Lazarevic, we suspended the sitting yesterday to give you a chance for another quick preparation for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning. It was a very useful decision. I managed to go through all the testimony of this witness, so I'll reduce probably my cross-examination and it will be less time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vasovic. Let me introduce myself for the record. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and I'm defending Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin, together with my colleagues, and I will be cross-examining you now on his behalf. I notice that you do have some experience testifying before this Tribunal, so perhaps this warning may not be necessary in your case, but still I'm going to ask you to make a small pause before starting your answer, after I finish asking my question, so that we don't have an overlap in the transcript. Can we start, then?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, reading -- having read your statement that you gave on the 23rd of April, 2007, I noticed that you stated that on the 13th of July, in the evening, sometime after 2000 hours, you had decided to go to the farming co-op in Kravica. As I read on, I realised that it was already dark at that time. And based on some other information that had come in during this trial, shouldn't it really read "2200 hours"? Shouldn't that be the time when you actually set off?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dusk when we set off. When we arrived, it was already dark. I can't really orient myself in time, but that was summertime so it's possible it might have been 2200 hours, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, I cannot press the point. I suppose you didn't really look at your watch to --

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. The next thing I would like to ask you pertains to the moment when you and Miladin Jovanovic, as indicated in your statement, and Jovan Nikolic, you arrived at the farming co-op in Kravica. On that occasion, to the best of your recollection, was there any other person in the car? I'm referring to Kosan Eric, aka Misa. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there, Kosan Eric, aka Misa, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And according to your statement, at that point, some uniformed persons came out of the dark, pointed their rifle at Jovan, and asked him to give them a hand guarding the prisoners. Do you recall having said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we got out of the car, Jovan Nikolic and I were to the right, and Jovan set off. He was the first. A uniformed soldier came out from the dark. There were others in the dark, so we couldn't see them. And they asked Jovan to join the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine, fair enough. I merely asked you whether you recall this part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that person that you saw coming out and stepping in front of Jovan Nikolic, that person wore a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he wore black overalls, but it was dark so you couldn't really see any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Do you remember that on the 5th or [as interpreted] the 6th, perhaps you don't know the exact date yourself, but it is in the documents here, that you testified in the Kravica case before the State Court in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Vasovic, you are going too fast. Please slow down so that we avoid problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll keep this in mind. I'll try to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's more the witness than you, but it's both of you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to correct the transcript. At page 3, line 20, I said -- I said "the 5th of the sixth month," and that means June, obviously, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, do you remember that in your testimony in that case, when the prosecutor, Mr. Ipaj [phoen] asked you about this, you also stated that the soldier who stepped in front of you wore a black uniform. This is what I was able to hear from the audiotape of the proceedings. You said it was a uniform, black overall. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you were also asked questions about the defence counsel, Ozren Kajaksic [phoen], and you also told her that it was a single-colour black uniform; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That soldier who approached Mr. Nikolic and yourself, did he introduce himself, state his name, full name?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, because the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't state his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did this soldier perhaps say what unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to see any insignia on this solid black uniform that would make it possible for you to conclude what unit this soldier belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't see the insignia. I don't even know whether there were any insignia, because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you testified -- well, I don't want to repeat all of that, but when you testified in the Kravica case, do you remember that when Ozren Kajaksic, the defence counsel, asked you about the insignia on the uniforms, that you gave the same answer that you have just given us?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I gave the same answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you were together with Jovan Nikolic, when that soldier came out?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You did not get separated from him?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not at any distance to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So, in principle, you were present during this incident involving Jovan Nikolic and this soldier in the black uniform; can we say that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you were able to hear and to see the same things that Jovan Nikolic was able to hear and see?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, did you hear that soldier in black uniform ask Jovan Nikolic to intervene in the Command in order to get a new shift or replacements for the troops deployed there?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you again. Do you remember that when the question that I just asked you was asked of you in the Kravica case by the defence counsel, Ozren Kajaksic, that you provided the same answer?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember, but if they asked me that, I'm sure that I gave the same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. I just don't think it's proper cross, when a witness gives an answer, to say, "You gave exactly the same answer in an earlier proceeding." I don't think it's necessary, when that hasn't been attacked or put in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't see any problem with this, I mean, honestly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't, either. Anyway, please proceed, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasovic, just a couple of questions. In your statement to the Beara Defence team, you say that you arrived in the co-op compound and that while you were there, you could see isolated shots. Were you able to determine the direction from which those shots were coming at that time?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't determine that, but we could hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You were asked about this at the Kravica case, and the prosecutor asked you a similar question and you provided a similar answer. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As you were on your way back to Bratunac by car, did Jovan Nikolic at any time say that the persons guarding the Muslim prisoners were members of the special police from Skelani; did Jovan Nikolic ever say anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that, and the next day when I was in contact with him again, he did not mention any units, any military formations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Jovan Nikolic at any time say that the soldiers you had seen in the compound -- I mean, that one soldier that you saw distinctly, and you had reason to believe there were others in the compound at the co-op in Kravica, did Jovan tell you they were asked him to inform their Command to provide replacements or reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: According to your statement to the Beara Defence, you stated that two days later, you heard from people in town that an incident had occurred, some killings had occurred in the warehouse in Kravica. Do you recall that? Do you remember when you heard that, from whom?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were talking. Different versions of that story were circulating, so I heard that somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, ten years later after these events from 1995, you cannot name the person who might have told you that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vasovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Just a couple of questions for you. Now, you've talked about this case several times in several statements, and now in several courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you gave a statement to SIPA [Realtime transcript read in error "CEPA"] on the 19th of June, 2005. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what SIPA means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not "CEPA." You gave a statement to the Bosnian authorities who were investigating this massacre at the Kravica warehouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement to the police of Republika Srpska. I don't know about other services. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if we could have it up here. It's -- I don't have the Defence 65 ter number for the 19 June 2005 statement. 3601. I'm sorry. It's our number. Well, in any event, you recall giving the statement to those authorities and signing it; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you promised to tell the truth in that statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were careful because it was a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was closer to the events than we are today; correct? Right, it was soon after these events happened?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me tell you what you said there about the shots: "Then we went to ZZ Kravica, since we have heard that something strange was going on there, that is, that people were being killed. While we were in ZZ Kravica, I heard single shots from the direction of the entrance to the warehouse or, more precisely, from the road. We immediately left ZZ Kravica, as our lives were in danger." Do you remember saying that to the investigators and signing that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The layout of the terrain, since we were closer to the building, indicated that the shots were coming from that side, but they could have been coming from the opposite side as well and what we heard was an echo. It doesn't mean that what I said -- what I assessed at the time is necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. My question was: Do you remember saying that to the investigators and signing that that was correct in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed the statement, but the statement was given when nobody asked me about my mental and physical capacity to give a statement. I was under stress because I had been taken out of a church of the same Trinity and taken to be interrogated. I felt depressed, and it's possible that I said a word out of turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So you don't want to stand by that answer you gave when you promised the tell the truth under penalty to the investigators of the RS?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard shots. I felt they were coming from the other side, and I confirm still today that I heard them. But it doesn't mean necessarily that it's correct. I was not in a position to decide where they were coming from, because it was dark, it was night. The sounds echoed from one hill to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So it was dark, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, just a question out of my curiosity. When the witness gave statements to the investigator, did he do so under penalty?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't have a translation of that, but I've seen it and I believe what it says is that -- I don't have a translation of that, but it's got language in there that under the regulations, you can -- you can be penalized if you're giving a false statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll check it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I have a different one, Your Honour, from the prior witness, but same investigating agency, and it states: "Pursuant to Article 86, paragraph 2 of the Law on Criminal Procedure of BH, I warn you that you have to tell the truth. You cannot hide anything. I hereby warn you that perjury constitutes a crime as specified by Article 235 of the Criminal Code for which sentence of imprisonment between six months and five years can be ruled." And that's on the first page of the statement form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: SIPA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we are talking about two different things. I just have in front of me -- I just have in front of me this statement. It's 19th of July -- 19th of June, 2005. Is this the same one that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So maybe my colleague can direct me to where he found this, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have a translation of the statement. My understanding is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I can find in this statement. What I can find is that this statement was provided to the Centre of Public Security in Bijeljina, Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, not to SIPA, which is the agency of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we can check it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I made an error there, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed in the meantime, and we can check it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In any event, Witness, what you told these investigators on 19th of June was that your best recollection at that time, three years ago, was that the shots were coming from the direction of the front of the warehouse or the road, but now you consider that might have been an echo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recollect most clearly the year 1995. I can even describe how a bullet travels. But I no longer can tell clearly whether it was an echo from the other side. I'm not sure at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the following day, on the 14th, you returned to Kravica warehouse around noon; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that time interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified about that in the State Court trial in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me just -- and you saw some soldiers there when you returned on the 14th, correct, or some men in uniform?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you described their uniforms. Let me read about how you described those. This is on page 12 of your testimony of 5th July 2006: "They were wearing camouflage uniforms, all," there is a word we can't read, "drab uniforms, these typical military uniforms. They were overalls, so in one piece, you know." Do you stand by that answer? Were you telling the truth when you said that in the State Court ?

utterances.speaker: PERICA VASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've always told the truth before that court and before your Tribunal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one issue. It might sound minor, but what Mr. Nicholls has just read to the witness is that he said "typical military uniforms." These typical military uniforms, this is what Mr. Nicholls just said, and I don't see the word "military" in line 19 on page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Sorry, thank you. Nothing further. Your Honours, sorry, I've got now a Republika Srpska witness form. I will still check, but it's got similar language, stating that: Pursuant to our paragraph 2, Article 86 of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Law on Criminal Procedure, the witness was instructed to tell the truth and not to hold back any information, in exactly similar language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Judge Kwon? Judge Prost? Judge Stole? Mr. Vasovic, we have finished with your testimony. You are free to go. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I thank you for having come over, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We tender some documents. Vasovic, Perica's statement given to our Defence team, the number is 2D 555, and it has been introduced into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objections. Objections from any of the Defence teams? None. So it is so admitted. Mr. Lazarevic, you don't have any documents, do you, to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to keep on this topic. I have the witness's statement in B/C/S. I've had some assistance. The warning that the statement is given under penalty is on page 2, as my friend asked. I can direct him to it. It's on page 2, above the witness's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Do you wish to add anything to that, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe just to help my friend. What Mr. Julian was quoting are relevant paragraphs of the Code of Criminal Conduct of the Bosnian Federation. However, when I look at the statement, the relevant paragraphs refer to the quote of the Criminal Proceedings of Republika Srpska. There are some differences. And furthermore, just to add to this discussion, this is not the statement made under oath, just to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise, do you have any documents, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. That concludes the testimony of Mr. Vasovic. Let's bring the next one, Mr. Mrkovic. And further, for the record, Mr. Elderkin now is present in the courtroom for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Mrkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as Presiding Judge, I welcome you to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence in this case, having been summoned as a Defence witness by Colonel Beara. Before you start your evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. The text is being handed to you now. Please read it in a way that we can hear you, and then that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. The Beara Defence team will go first. They will be followed by cross-examination with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, good morning. As you know, I'm John Ostojic, and I represent Ljubisa Beara with our team here.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Ljuban Mrkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, sir, and specifically in the mid-1990s, did you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share that with us? What was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: They called me "Mrki," derived from my last name, since my childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please give us your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of December, 1953, in Ljubinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just briefly, could you outline for us your educational background, the highest level you attained when and where, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary school in Ljubinje, my birthplace. After that, I went to the Secondary Aviation School, and then I continued with the Aviation Engineering School in Rajlovac. After that, I graduated from the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give us an idea, if you don't mind, Mr. Mrkovic. When exactly did you finish this aviation school; approximately the year or so?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a flying school. It's an engineering academy for the aviation engineering staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the year. There is a lot of noise around the witness that drowns the witness's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, they're having a little trouble hearing us, so thank you for moving up. If you could just give me the year again, please. We weren't able to hear it, so it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated the Aviation Engineering School in 1977 in Rajlovac, and the Command Staff Academy in 1990 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just briefly and to get a better flavour for your background and experience, can you share with us, from 1977, whether you were gainfully employed and where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked for a while in the aviation school in Sombor, and after that I worked the whole time in Rajlovac. After those two years in Sombor, I spent all of my other time in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a suburb of Sarajevo. During the war, it was a municipality six kilometres going away from the center of Sarajevo towards Ilijas and Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that from 1990, you attended a Command Staff. Can you tell me how, if at all, were employed from 1990 to 1992? Where were you gainfully employed, if at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1990 until 1992, I worked in the Aviation Engineering Academy in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us what you did, just generally speaking. What were some of your duties or responsibilities at that time while you were working with that engineering academy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that school I occupied many positions, from director of the school, reserve officer, head of the chair for the training of foreign nationals. I occupied many positions until 1992, including security chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And now can you tell us what you did subsequent to 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: After 1992, in fact in December 1991, I was the security organ in the aircraft manufacturing plant Orao, which is just next to the school in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that to describe some of your job duties there. How long did you work at the Orao airplane manufacturing plant? I know you said you started in December 1991. Up until what point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did your position at the Orao aircraft manufacturing plant stay the same throughout that period 1991 through 1997?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you told us briefly what you did. Can you share with us what your job duties and responsibilities were from December of 1991 up until the time you left the Orao manufacturing plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: That would take a long time, but I'll try to tell you very briefly. This aircraft manufacturing plant, Orao, is a company in the military business, as they called it before, the military industry, that dealt with repairs of engines of fighter planes, not only for the former Yugoslavia but for all the other countries in the region; Arab countries, England, the Netherlands and many other countries in the world. It was perhaps one of the strongest companies in that line of business in Europe. In 1992, in Orao, the technology was so advanced that the entire former Yugoslavia invested in that company, and for that reason my scope of work in that company was very complex. But, of course, with the secession of many republics, those republics kept a large number of aircraft and engines. Everybody tried to get hold of the documentation, of spare parts, and those were the most important things we were doing during the war in Bosnia, as far as the Orao company is concerned and my own work, to preserve the property, to preserve the documentation and the spare parts in the company, because it's still working. It operated throughout the war, and it's still in operation. It's not what it used to be, but it's still in the business.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear on the record, this Orao manufacturing plant was in Rajlovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you said, right outside of Sarajevo. And now tell us, more specifically -- please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned it, this company was next-door to the aviation garrison. The road was the only thing separating the two warring sides, so we can fairly say that the company was -- the plant was on the separation line itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- you described briefly what some of the assets were and your role in protecting that documentation and preserving that documentation through the war. Can you give us a little more specificity as to what type of assets it was that you were protecting or trying to secure at that point? Was it machine -- was it the actual physical aeroplane, was it machine parts, or anything to the best of your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first objective that we had in the management of this plant was to keep the personnel intact, because without the personnel all the machinery was worth nothing. So we wanted to keep the people working. Our next task and obligation was to preserve the property that we had, and of course to keep intact the documentation that had been produced by generations before us, because this was very sensitive technology. So this was -- these were our key tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, how many people were at this manufacturing plant, say, at the time that you arrived in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: In December 1991, there were about 600 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you see that number decrease over the course of the three years thereafter up and through until the end of 1995, if we could use that as a time frame? And that would be in light of the Dayton Accords, approximately.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, once the fighting started when the war broke out, many people from the facility were in Sarajevo. Some left, fled abroad to Belgrade, and in order to continue our production process, we tried to get the people back. And then at one point we had maybe 30 to 40 people working there, and they kept the operation going. But after that, the number increased to 150, 200 people. Nowadays, the facility employees about 300 people. But it had been too cumbersome, so in April we started with maybe 30, 40 people, and then in 1994 we had about 150, 200 people who came to the very frontline to do their job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, just so we have the correct year, when you say "April," you're saying -- and you correct me if I'm wrong, I don't mean to lead on this, but what year in April did you mean -- April of what year, that it was reduced to approximately 30 to 40 people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think the interpreter --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know, and maybe I can just clarify on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, I think you said "2002," but is that when you were there, 2002, or really are we talking about April 1992, when the actual war broke out? Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I said "2002," I misspoke. 1992. In 2002, I wasn't there at all. 1992. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay, because the interpreter certainly understood you, because they first said "1992," and realised you misspoke and said, "2002," but that isn't really important, so we can move on. What was specifically your job title from 1992 through --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No need. Thank you, though. Sir, what was your specific job title from 1992 through 1995 at the Orao aircraft manufacturing plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: My job title was security organ in the Orao [Realtime transcript read in error "Orahovo"] aircraft manufacturing plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, how long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1991 until 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm just -- because obviously I think I'm overlapping, and I do apologise for that. On the transcript, on page 22, line 3, and just so it's clear, it's not "Orahovo aeroplane manufacturing plant," it's simply O-R-A-O, Orao aircraft manufacturing plant. I don't know if it's necessary, but we'd like to have as clean a transcript as possible, so thank you and I apologise for that intervention, Mr. President. Sir, can you tell us how many people worked with you in that capacity or within the security organ of the Orao aircraft manufacturing plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I, and there was another clerk or desk officer who left for Belgrade later, and there was another desk officer there. So never more than two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And from 1990 -- or let's specifically say 1995, to the best of your recollection, do you know how many people worked with you within that security organ in the capacity that you have described that you were so employed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Going back generally to the Orao aircraft manufacturing plant, can you tell me if you recall, between 1992 and 1995, what was the ethnic composition mix, if any, of the employees within the plant? Was it strictly a Serbian ethnicity or did you also have other ethnicities within the plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already spoken about that before this Tribunal in the General Milosevic case. The personnel in Orao was multiethnic. I don't have the exact date now, but there were several Muslims and Croats working on the same jobs that were done also by Serbs, so there was no division, no separation. One of my tasks was to monitor them, to work with them, and it was in the interests of Orao and everybody else to keep those people working there. We managed to do that throughout the war, but unfortunately now I hear that some people, some Croats and a Muslim, left for Canada, went abroad, because they're such good experts. But that was because of low salaries, so the management and I really feel sorry about that. But I have to stress here, there were not only Serbs; there were Serbs, Croats, Muslims working there at the plant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could you Mr. Ostojic please switch off the microphone when the witness is responding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll do that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, I'd hate to put you on the spot, but do you remember any names of such employees who were of Muslim or Croat ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the names that stuck in my memory is Saban Tabak, a Muslim. His wife was in Ilidza, and so were her children. We helped her to get to Belgrade and to come back. Then Zeljko Juric, Ivan Jurkovic, a Croat. Well, 15 years have passed, but these are the names of people who worked in the plant at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help understand the function further of the plant and maybe of the hierarchy of the plant. Who was the director or the main person at the plant from 1991 through 1997? If you can give me the title, and then if you remember the name and if it changed, share that with us, if you don't mind. So, in essence, what was the main person at the Orao manufacturing plant? What was his job title called?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, the former JNA was still in existence, and the late Laza Grbic was the director, and then it was Colonel Milovanovic. In 1992, they withdrew to Belgrade, in accordance with the order stating that all members of the JNA should withdraw to Belgrade, and then it was Milan Prica. He was the director throughout this time from 1992 until 1997. And let me just clarify one thing. In the former JNA, the Air Force Command -- the logistics in the Air Force Command appointed the director.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you could perhaps ask the witness to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, we did not obtain a complete translation of what you just said, so the Court's asked me and the interpreters have asked us to ask you to just repeat the part where you started to clarify certain things, and you stated: "In the former JNA, the Air Force Command ... ," and then there's some hyphens: "The logistics in the Air Force Command appointed a director." And, sir, I know we're all nervous here and I'm probably just as nervous as you are talking in front of this panel and these other lawyers, but just relax and take a drink of water. We'll walk through all this so we have a better understanding of what you did in that time period, and so if you would be kind enough to repeat for us what you were starting to say about logistics and the director of this Orao Aeroplane manufacturing plant, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1992, April 1992, the director of the Orao facility was Colonel Vladeta Milanovic, and pursuant to the order of the former Yugoslavia that the army should withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he complied with it and he and some part of the management of the plant withdrew to Belgrade in 1992, in April. Once Milovanovic was gone, Milovanovic appointed one of the competent persons in the plant, Milan Prica, to be his stand-in. He had a degree in aviation engineering. He had been working in the plant for sometime at that time, and it was not clear to me whether the government of Republika Srpska was set up or not, but at any time Milan Prica had this job. And in September 1992, the Ministry of Defence appointed Milan Prica the director of the plant, and this order existed, it was there in Orao. And throughout the time that Orao plant operated, the logistics of Republika Srpska provided professional assistance and proposed any changes in the plant. And the Ministry of Defence issued decisions to appoint people to appoint a director of this Orao plant. I hope that I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- very much so, and thank you for that. Now, if I could turn specifically, sir -- if I can turn specifically, sir, to your job duties in the security organ, did you conduct or perform any counter-intelligence work while you were working at the Orao aeroplane manufacturing plant from 1992 through 1995, or '7, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already stated that it was my basic task to carry out counter-intelligence protection of the Orao plant and its staff. 80 per cent of my job was doing this and, of course, protecting the property, the people, and all the other assets that were there in the plant. If you want me to clarify that, I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I respectfully would, because I'd like to get a better appreciation for what you did in your capacity while performing counter-intelligence work as a security -- in the security organ. So, yes, please, if you don't mind, tell me, to the best of your recollection, what were your day-to-day or week-to-week duties and responsibilities in conducting counter-intelligence work while at the Orao plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a nutshell, the plant had huge assets, a lot of those documents that had been put together over the years. In 1992, we started doing the repairs on MiG 29, one of the most advanced aircraft at the time, and all this had to be protected and preserved. When republics broke away, you can imagine the kind of pressure that was exerted by all the countries in the region to get the documents, to get the spare parts, to recruit some people to make them transfer to work for them. I think that I and the rest of the management of the Orao plant managed to preserve this and that we are one of the few factories or plants in Republika Srpska that operated nonstop, and I think it is a great success that this management can claim for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. More specifically, if I may ask you, did you conduct counter-intelligence operations or investigations specifically against the Bosnian Muslim or Croat employees or were you non-discriminatory in your efforts to protect the assets of the Orao aeroplane manufacturing plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we paid no attention to that in Orao, to the ethnic background of people. What we cared about was that people should do their job and to be adequately rewarded for doing it properly. Throughout the war, after the war, in 1995, this has been our goal. Oh, now I recall another Bosniak, Jako, and there was another person who was married to a Croat, Andja, some people who still work in Orao. So it was really not our goal to do that. Of course, we had to keep an eye on everyone to prevent any surprises, but this was the job of the security organ, to watch out for any such surprises. But there was no pressure on them. Well, at one point they had a nickname for me, "Welfare worker," because I helped them more than I did Serbs. So that would happen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure you mentioned a Bosniak by the name of Jako, and I didn't catch the name when you uttered it, but if you remember, if you just have it so we could have it in the transcript, the gentleman that you just recollected as you were sitting here. His last name, if you will.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Bosnjak, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, did you also conduct any intelligence or counter-intelligence efforts within the Orao manufacturing plant prior to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally some people were being processed, checked. We ran checks. In some cases, we were successful; in others, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You told us during your testimony that the Ministry of Defence would appoint a director, and then you told us how Logistics was involved in terms of the physical assets, professionally speaking, of the Orao manufacturing plant. Share with us now, if you will, to whom did you report during that period of 1992 through 1995 or 1997? And the reason I'm -- we want to focus up to 1995, but if it changed during that time period, please just enlighten us and then we'll clarify that. So I'm not sure that it has, but to the extent that it may have, to whom you reported, you can share that with us as well, sir. So from whom did you report from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I reported up the command-and-control -- chain of command and control to the director of the plant - I was his subordinate - and to the security administration. That was along the professional line of command, because I was under the Security Administration of the Army of Republika Srpska. Those reports were sometimes daily reports, sometimes weekly, and we had to submit reports every month. Daily reports were submitted every day to the plant director, because the security organ was linked, in military terms, to the director of the plant, in military terms. In professional terms, it was subordinate to the Security Administration. Let me clarify one more thing. Since I was in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, many of the reports that I sent to the Security Administration were actually also copied to the security section of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, because I was in their area of responsibility. So it was done up the chain of command in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we've heard a lot of evidence or some evidence here about control and command and the professional aspect of it, as well as the six corps that existed in the former Bosnian area, and including the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Can you be more specific, though, and tell me with whom -- if there was one individual during any longer period of time, did you report to in the -- or within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, I supplied intelligence that I obtained to the chief of the security section, Mr. Marko Lugonja, and of course I also sent it to the Main Staff, or sometimes I agreed with him that he, because he had so much more experience than me and he was responsible for that in his area of responsibility, so I sent it to him, and then he would forward it. It would happen quite often. I would report to -- I would provide my reports to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps regarding intelligence that I obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe if you could help us here, and this isn't -- sorry. Maybe if you could help us, I think you said "Marko Lugonja"; right? Would you mind spelling that, because in the transcript that you perhaps can see in front of you, there's a different spelling, and I just want to make sure we're talking about the same individual. And if you don't remember how to spell it, sir, that's okay, I think the Prosecution and we all know who you're referring to. And since you're looking at the transcript, if you look at page 30, at line 20, so just from the left-hand side, line 20.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Marko, M-A-R-K-O, L-U-G-O-N-J-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, interpreters, and thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at any time from 1991 through 1997, did you report to anyone else at the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, other than Marko Lugonja? Was there someone who replaced him or were you given instructions to report to someone else within the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You shared with us briefly the types or how often you would send reports. These reports were generated from your office in Rajlovac in Orao manufacturing plant, and you would send it directly to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and/or to the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, share with us, if you will, if you know the gentleman by the name of Ljubisa Beara? Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's lay a little more foundation if we can for that. Tell us when, where, and in what capacity did you meet Mr. Beara, to the extent that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you the exact dates, but I think it was sometime in November or December 1992. That was when Ljubisa Beara was appointed the chief of the Security Administration in the army of Republika Srpska. I think that was when we first met.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm not asking for any more precision on your part than that which you can honestly recall here. Do you remember, in 1995, more specifically, and even prior to that, if Mr. Beara visited the Orao manufacturing plant in Rajlovac? Physically, did he visit you or your plant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall the details, but I know that he would come very often. Every time when he visited the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, he would visit the Orao plant. I can't tell you whether it was 10 or 20 times in the course of those three years, but I know for a fact that he came very often; not only Ljubisa Beara, but others would also come visit, help us in any way, logistics, operations. But at any rate, people would come, and Ljubo Beara would visit the plant very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, and we can take whatever time period, but we'd like to focus on 1995, do you remember if he stayed there for a day or longer, or a short period of time? Was there any consistency to the visits that he made to Orao there at Rajlovac to visit you guys at the plant? Do you remember if he stayed there ever longer than a day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was our practice to meet every month with all the security organs in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, so all of us would get together and then we would do our analyses, the monthly analyses. I can't really tell you how many times Mr. Beara attended those meetings, but before I came here, I checked in my notebooks. On the 5th of July, 1995, Ljubisa Beara convened this monthly meeting at Dragutinovic in the Ilijas Brigade, and I and all the other organs got this dispatch or a telegram from the Main Staff. Well, you can find this in the documents. I know that we had this meeting on the 5th of July in Ilijas, and I know that Ljubo Beara stayed there two or three days, because we pressed him to stay longer, and I know that he said -- well, Ljubo was always in a hurry. He said, "There's another frontline opening up in Krajina." I remember that meeting in 1995, when Ljubo told us that new frontlines are being opened up in Krajina, in Sarajevo, here, there, everywhere, and I know that we stayed there for a long time. And he said that he was going to Krajina. I don't know whether he went there or not, but I do know that he always tried to leave as soon as possible. And I'm sure that on the 5th of July, we were in Ilijas, at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Mrkovic. That's a lot of information, and I'm going to try to dissect it. You're getting a little ahead of me, which is fine, and thank you very much for that, because it helps all of us keep focused. You mentioned in your testimony that -- about some notes that you checked in your notebook. And I think if everyone just focuses on page 6 of line 32 [sic] of the transcript, you said you'd check in "my notebooks." What notebooks are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had a notebook where I wrote about all those various meetings. It's now pretty faded and old, but I leafed through it when I was invited to testify here. And yesterday, in my room, when I lay down, I believe -- I thought about that meeting, and I believe it was held on the 5th of July in Ilijas. I remember I had met Vojin Dragutinovic about a year ago in Zvornik. He calls on me often, and he had -- he reminded me of that lunch that we were supposed to have and, in the end, didn't. But at the end of the day, every brigade has its documentation, and that dispatch must be there. If it reached me, it must have reached everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just help us understand where Ilijas is. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Ilijas is to the west of Sarajevo, 21 kilometres from Rajlovac. You go on the road to Zenica, 21, 22, 23 kilometres, depending on where you measure from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just so we have a better understanding, can you tell us, in July of 1995, who was Vojin Dragutinovic, and what capacity did he hold with the Ilijas Brigade, if at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Vojin Dragutinovic was the chief of the security of the Ilijas Brigade, so he had the equivalent of my job in the aircraft manufacturing plant, in the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, forgive me for asking, but I need to know. Do you have your notebook with you at the hotel or here in the Netherlands, because you referred to it and I just --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's back home somewhere; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's currently in Zvornik. It's a small notebook, perhaps the only piece of paper that I leafed through recently to look through the various meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, if I can just ask you, sir, to please don't throw that notebook or piece of paper away, because we may ask you to produce that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that okay, can we ask you to do that, sir? Just because you finish your testimony here today, we're asking that you still preserve that, and we'll, with the Prosecution, find a mechanism with which we can obtain it if we're still interested. So we're asking you to kindly preserve and not throw away that notebook or that piece of paper. Okay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I may even have the original document inviting me to that meeting, inviting all the security chiefs to that meeting. I'm not sure, but I may just have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that. The same, if we can request that same thing with this document. Whatever you have, in essence, if you can just retain it, and then we'll be calling upon you after we testify so that we can possibly examine or get a copy of those documents. So we're asking you nicely to just kindly don't throw it away. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrkovic. Now, let's go back to this meeting on or about the 5th of July, 1995, in Ilijas. What was the purpose of the meeting, to the extent that you recall? I know you mentioned it was a monthly meeting, but give us, if you will, an overview of the types of things that were discussed during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard after all this time. There was a regular item on the agenda that was always included, and that was an analysis of the work of security organs for the past month and the evaluation of the situation on the ground. Now, I really can't remember the rest of that meeting. Anything I would try to recall would not be reliable. It's been 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe with the help of some of those documents or original documents and notebooks that you have, it may help you refresh your recollection, but my question is really generally, and I think you've answered it, the things that you would generally discuss at these monthly meetings. Can you share with us who, generally again, would partake or participate in these monthly meetings that you identified, similar to the one that occurred on or about the 5th of July in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all chiefs of security from brigades would attend, sometimes security chiefs of battalions, the security chief of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and there would be someone from the Security Administration. Specifically on that occasion, it was Ljubo Beara. I know that from that notebook. I know that on that occasion, it was Ljubisa Beara from the Security administration. And the topic of that meeting was the extremely difficult military and political situation in Republika Srpska, the Sarajevo theatre of war. Intelligence told us that various units were being transferred from one frontline to another frontline and so on. Then the situation in Krajina was very difficult because units were arriving from Croatia, from here and there, and preparing for action. I think that was the main topic of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you mentioned several specific areas relating to theaters of war. Do you remember, to the best of your recollection, at that time whether there was any activity that was taking place in the Bihac war theatre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the intelligence that I received, the offensive was in Bihac. There was an offensive in Bihac. But what was specifically going on, I couldn't tell you. All I know is that there was that offensive at Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it might be a good time to take a break. We're going to move on to a similar but more specific aspect of his testimony. If the Court permits, I'll ask that the break starts now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, with your permission, the Court's permission, the OTP and I have had a brief discussion during the break, and we'd like to ask of the witness a couple more questions in connection with a document that he seems to have in his possession. So if it's permissible with you, and the Prosecution believes, as you'll hear from the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, good morning still. How are you? Sir, with respect to the document or notebook or piece of paper that you had, my learned friends from the Prosecution have asked me whether or not they can send their investigator, who I believe is currently around Sarajevo, to your home to pick up this material so that, in their view, they wouldn't have to call you back, if necessary, to talk about that document. Do you know whether that document and/or notebook is at your home, and is there anyone, with your permission, if you grant it, that we can give that to one of the investigators from the OTP? Or if you have another preference, you can share that with us as well.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: When I come back to Bosnia, I can enable the investigators to have it as soon as possible. That can be the day after tomorrow or tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I would just ask that you, you know, write down what you give them, and we'll talk about it. So if you would be kind enough to meet with the Prosecution and myself after you've concluded or completed your testimony, we'll make arrangements for that. Thank you very much, Mr. Mrkovic. Now, sir, I'd like to go back to this discussion that we were having on your recollection with respect to the 5th of July, 1995, where Mr. Beara was present. What I'd like to know is: Do you remember if, prior to July, like in June or May, did Mr. Beara make visits at all at the Orao manufacturing plant or at Ilidza at any time, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be 100 per cent sure, but I believe Mr. Ljubisa was at the plant at the time and he was in the Ilidza Brigade. I think he even refueled at my station in the plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me ask you a little bit more, and then we'll get into the sum and substance of your testimony in connection with this meeting on the 5th of July. But before I ask you that, you mentioned in the beginning that you testified in the Dragomir Milosevic case, and we have the date, sir, just so the record is clear, and I don't think it's an issue in dispute, that it's the 12th and 13th of July, 2007. Does that sound about right, almost approximately a year ago that you testified in that case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was summertime, but the date is certainly in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help us with this, because in our documents that the Prosecution gives us, they give us a specific collection that they've called either the Srebrenica collection or the Drina Corps collection. But relating to that other case, do you know if that involved the Sarajevo Romanija Corps at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know. In all the documents I received, both as a security organ and in intelligence, did not indicate that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was in any way involved or that it performed any operations in the area of the Drina Corps. I could not find that anywhere in the papers or any information that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I was actually asking for another reason, in the hopes that maybe the Prosecution may have the Sarajevo Romanija Corps documents and they might be able to assist us in finding the documents that you were referencing, but thank you. And, in any event, we'll move on. Sir, at any time did you and I review intercepts that purport to have your name or a conversation that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean, did I review?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did I, sir, show you last night a video which had your conversation -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: That, that's so. You showed it to me yesterday. Last night, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, sir, did you at any time have a discussion with myself, Mr. Nikolic, any attorneys or investigators on the Beara Defence team, with respect to any intercepts or purported intercepts that may bear your name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like, with the Court's permission, for us to call up specifically this one intercept that's dated the 10th of July, 1995, and it bears the number T001-1340. Mr. President, this was a document that was disclosed to us by the Prosecution. We did not have an English translation. We spent several hours trying to translate these documents this morning. My learned friend from the Prosecution was kind enough to give us all the English translations of the intercepted material within that disc, so we do also have, I believe, at least one copy. We will furnish that for the Court so that you have it in evidence as well, the English as well as the B/C/S version of the intercept. And if we may now have that video or that tape broadcast, and it's a very short video. It goes specifically under our 2D 557, the transcript in B/C/S. We will attach the English version as it was provided to us by the Prosecution this morning, and again it's T001-1340.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we stop it, please. And let me -- before I ask you, Mr. Mrkovic, a question: We have the transcript, and we provided it to the interpreters. I thought they were going to read along a little bit with us. If they don't have the English version, we have another copy they can. I just want to ask the witness specifically if he recognises any of the voices on the tape as a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, we were not seeing anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because it's audio, it's only an audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you said it's a very short video. You did mention audio, but you also mentioned video.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that. It's strictly audio.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a precise reference or at least an indication how we are supposed to find it among -- what words it begins with or something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did. If I can directly answer that, it begins with an unknown male that states: "The beginning of the conversation was not recorded." On top it has the date of the 10th of July, 1995, at 1854 hours. The internal number, if I could share it, is CD-96-17-04/06/021, they should have and as I'm reading just the top portion of that from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And with the Court's permission, I'm not sure if the Court has the entire English version yet, but we were just going to have them read it as it appears on the transcript and as it's playing for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If it would help, Your Honours, I have a couple of extra copies in English that I could pass up to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. That would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may -- oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Again, another practical suggestion is it may be difficult for the interpreters to follow along at the speed of the tape, and we had envisaged as well using perhaps some of these materials and to have one of our team, who we can call down here, to follow on the ELMO just to show as the tape is playing, line by line, where we are in the English. It would only take five minutes to bring her down, if that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know that it's necessary. I'll defer if that's the better practice, because I'm focusing only on page 5 of 8. I was going to ask that we merely read along. The interpreters need not translate those first four or so pages, but we do have it in front, and we were going to stop on page 5. But I did need the witness to confirm whether he identifies any of the participants in the conversation. But I would be more than happy to have the OTP help us, if that's what they desire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand, the OTP might be using this later on again or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It is being played now, then no. But if it wasn't going to be played, we have somebody upstairs who was going to come down to help us follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's follow Mr. Ostojic's suggestion for the time being and then we'll see if it becomes more practical to adopt your suggestion, then we'll do so. Yes, Mr. Ostojic. So we need to go to page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can just play a little bit of the tape so I could lay a little foundation for who the persons may be on the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if we could start from the beginning, and I'll ask them kindly to stop. And, then Mr. Mrkovic, I'm going to proceed and ask you a couple of questions. Please, if we can play the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "May your father fuck you. Ljuban, holy shit. UNKNOWN MALE: He is there slightly more than before. LJUBAN: There's slightly more? UNKNOWN MALE: Of course. LJUBAN: Who else is there? UNKNOWN MALE: Nobody, just him. LJUBAN: Just him? UNKNOWN MALE: Yes, yes. LJUBAN: Anything you on your side? UNKNOWN MALE: Nothing, just a few jobs here and there. LJUBAN: Yes, screw it. UNKNOWN MALE: According to the old pattern as they all say. LJUBAN: Old pattern, new customs, fuck."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, Mr. President. I actually thought, and I thought I was clear, we didn't need it translated up until the fifth page, and I apologise for obviously some of the language. I just need to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. Mrkovic, if I may, do you recognise any of the individuals that are speaking on this tape, the audiotape that we have just played?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us if you recognise yourself at all on this --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can assume that, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit changed, but it could be. Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person who has been identified, at least in the translated version of the intercept by the OTP, as an unknown male? As you sit here and listen, unless you need to listen to more of it, do you know who that other individual was at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's Zoran from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Zoran Stankovic, I believe, an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, we're going to play the tape, and I believe there's no need for the interpreters to read it for us, since I think the Court has a copy, and we will provide a copy of that. And just to assist them, we would like to have the tape played, and when we get to approximately page 5, we'll ask that it be stopped. So if we could continue with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. And where are we supposed to start reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would prefer the interpreters to follow, and then we can also follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We were just trying to short circuit it, but that's fair, Your Honour. We'll have them read it as it's going along, and I'll ask them to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least the initial part, and then we can follow ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can we start again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "How is it going up there?" Can the interpreters know where we are reading from? Where have we started now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Stop, please. And just because the interpreters asked for assistance, I was trying to find it. If they turn to page 2 of 8, in the lower third portion of the document, it starts with: "Let me tell you, I should come this Friday." I believe that's where the audio is right now, so they can follow at that point, unless the Court prefers us to start a little earlier. Thank you. So if we can start the tape, and for the interpreters' benefit we are again on page 2 of 8, the lower third portion of the document with: "Let me tell you, I should come this Friday." If we can play --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ljuban, let me tell you, I should come this Friday. There is a car, Toso's car. Fuck it, I've had it up to here. It should be brought here from Belgrade and then I could drop by. UNKNOWN MALE: Right. You should have a few drinks. LJUBAN: I will, as soon as I can get going, promise. UNKNOWN MALE: Hello. Hello, sir. UNKNOWN MALE: Hello. LJUBAN: Hello. UNKNOWN MALE: Hello, Mrki. LJUBAN: Where have you been? I haven't heard a word for three days? You are constantly changing numbers. UNKNOWN MALE: And you find me just as you have left me every time you call. LJUBAN: Not really, swear to god. UNKNOWN MALE: By god this is so, you can see it. LJUBAN: Swear to god, I called yesterday, they told me on 250 to call here. Said he wasn't here but there. Screw it, I say, never can catch him. UNKNOWN MALE: It's all one door next to another. LJUBAN: Well, fine, I'm not gone. Get those men to get up and call you. Screw it. UNKNOWN MALE: Ljuban, what's up with you? UNKNOWN MALE: Nothing to brag about. Fuck it. LJUBAN: There's not enough of it around, either. UNKNOWN MALE: With you? LJUBAN: Well, I'm fine, let me tell you. UNKNOWN MALE: How it's's the boss? LJUBAN: He's okay otherwise. UNKNOWN MALE: Where are you calling from? LJUBAN: My own place. UNKNOWN MALE: Down there? LJUBAN: M'mm-hmm. UNKNOWN MALE: Since we are talking, there's something else. LJUBAN: Yes, yes, only if I should go to another place to -- why anything else? UNKNOWN MALE: Well, I would like to have someone else hear that. LJUBAN: M'mm-hmm. UNKNOWN MALE: It's not urgent, when it's convenient to you. LJUBAN: When will you be there? UNKNOWN MALE: I'm here all the time. LJUBAN: At that number? All right, listen, I'll go to that other, you know, secure line. UNKNOWN MALE: All right. LJUBAN: Then we'll speak. Any news from you? UNKNOWN MALE: Nothing special. LJUBAN: Nothing special? UNKNOWN MALE: Yes. LJUBAN: Fuck it. What was I going to say? Forgot it. UNKNOWN MALE: I haven't seen him. I don't know. LJUBAN: You haven't? Well fuck it, we'll see. UNKNOWN MALE: I haven't been up there at all. LJUBAN: Well yeah, and I have been thinking I should go up Thursday or Friday to take that IDA. Fuck that IDA, I've had it. UNKNOWN MALE: Take what? LJUBAN: That Ascona of ours. UNKNOWN MALE: Where is it? LJUBAN: It's finished up there. UNKNOWN MALE: Is it? LJUBAN: Well, it is, fuck people. UNKNOWN MALE: Easy. LJUBAN: Tell me you can pass 100.000, so I say let me do 50 and Toso and his team 50. Is that fair? UNKNOWN MALE: Yes. LJUBAN: Is that right? UNKNOWN MALE: You are right. LJUBAN: Beara says that it's not impossible, not possible. There you go. UNKNOWN MALE: So you just say under repair and that's it. LJUBAN: I should. They're all spies, man, they see and hear everything. UNKNOWN MALE: Fuck them. LJUBAN: You cannot hide anything from them. Beara came and stayed with us for three or four days. UNKNOWN MALE: Really? LJUBAN: Yes, there you go. UNKNOWN MALE: What did you -- LJUBAN: We were doing something, fuck. But we were not very successful. UNKNOWN MALE: Something around your house or in the neighbourhood? LJUBAN: Well, both. UNKNOWN MALE: M'mm-hmm. LJUBAN: Everywhere, and --"

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
