utterances.text: We can stop there. And if the Court wishes, we can [indiscernible] the next three pages but if we can just focus on here, I do have a couple questions with respect to Mr. Mrkovic on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, this looks as if, at least on the written transcript, that there were two conversations within one on the 10th of July, 1995, at approximately 1854, and, sir, I know that yesterday you were somewhat troubled and embarrassed because of some of the profanity that was used, and we'll address that in a moment with you. But the second part of the conversation, where it starts: "Hello," and, "Hello, Mrki," can you tell us if you recognise who that unknown male if it's the same one that you identified Zoran as you previously testified about? Do you recognise the unknown male on the second portion of this tape?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Somebody from the Main Staff, from the Security Administration, but I'm not sure who it was. I really couldn't, on the basis of this conversation, now say who this person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't claim who that person is. It is my voice. These are the things that I said, but I'm not sure about the other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time on the 10th of July, 1995, in speaking with this other individual that has been identified as "Unidentified male person," you state at page 5 of 8, the lower portion: "You can't hide anything from them. Beara came and stayed with us for three, four days." Do you remember hearing that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I just want to make sure we're clear. At or about the 10th of July, does this conversation assist in refreshing your recollection that Ljubisa Beara was in or near the area -- I'm going to miss pronounce it again -- Rajlovac for three or four days, or three to four days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a conversation that was intercepted on the 10th of July. We had this meeting on the fifth in Ilijas. I'm sure that I have this document in my possession, and we'll arrange for this document to be sent to you. This is the invitation to the meeting. Ljubisa stayed there a couple of days, and from this intercept you can see that -- well, I wouldn't have said that he was there if it hadn't been the case. I came here to tell the truth. I can't recall this conversation. Well, it was a long time ago, I had so many conversations, but I do believe this is an intercepted conversation in which I participated. And I apologise for those profanities that I used. Those were the times -- war times, so I am a little bit embarrassed about it. But what I really said was that he was there. This was not something that we hid. He was there from the 5th until the 8th or 9th. I can't really say that. And I think that he went for Krajina or somewhere, because he would always be in a hurry to go to Krajina. That was his usual pattern. He would visit the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and then he would go on to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you, before we get into the discussion of Mr. Beara possibly going to Krajina, let me ask you: What were you guys discussing there? I mean, you mentioned things like Asconas, and then you ask about, "Can you pass 100.000," and then there's a discussion about "is 50 fair," et cetera. Can you tell us an idea, to the best of your recollection, what is it you folks are talking about during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only make an assumption as to what it was. Since we had quite a lot of money in the aircraft plant and we supplied, with vehicles and fuel, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and also the Main Staff, so if anyone came to visit, they would get fuel. This Ascona was from the Security Administration and the engine broke down because there was some oil problems. So we transferred it to Sarajevo, the repair facility. It was repaired, and the garage guaranteed that it would go 100.000 kilometres without any glitches, and this is a joke that I made. I said, "Let's say -- let me do 50.000, and Toso, his team can do 50.000." So we were talking about this car that was purportedly able to make 100.000 kilometres without any breakdowns. So we're talking about this car. And now where it says Beara didn't give it, well, he didn't want us to spend a lot, so he didn't give us. So this whole conversation is about repairing a vehicle. This is a reference to 100.000 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, you just testified, in your prior answer, that you believe or recall, and help us understand this better, that after Mr. Beara left Rajlovac, that he went to the Krajina front. And before the break, you were telling us that there was actually the theatre of war occurring simultaneously both in Sarajevo and in Krajina, and then I think I asked you relating to Bihac. Do you have specific recollection, as you sit here today, whether or not you had a conversation with Mr. Beara and where he would be going after he left Rajlovic [sic] on or about July 9th or so, 1995? Or Rajlovac. I keep -- I misspoke when I said "Rajlovic." It's "Rajlovac." I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I think at that meeting, he said after Sarajevo he had to go to Krajina. I think that is what was said at the meeting. This was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, because it's important, do you have a clear recollection of that or you're just merely making an assumption because of his past prior habits that you may have seen, or seen him going from your area to, let's say, Krajina, or Bihac, or any other area? Do you, as you're sitting here, have a specific recollection of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that with 100 per cent certainty, so I can't say it with 100 per cent certainty. But he mentioned Krajina, he mentioned going to Krajina. Now, as to where he actually went, I couldn't really tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and we're just looking for your best recollection. Let me switch the topic for a moment and ask you a couple of things about the humanitarian convoys. Were you familiar at all, during that time, 1992 through 1995, or did you have any information relating to the humanitarian convoys that were passing through your area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Milosevic trial, I said this: Humanitarian aid passed into Sarajevo regularly through Kiseljak and Ilidza, into Sarajevo through Kasindolska Street, very often. In 1992, it was especially the case, as it was in 1993. And then at one point, I think it was the Ilidza Brigade searched one of the convoys. I don't know whether it was the MUP or the military, but I know that they found weapons and military equipment in there. And after that, those convoys were scaled down a little bit. Advanced notice was required and searches were also needed, because this was one channel of supplying Sarajevo with weapons and military equipment. The convoys continued. It was a little bit more difficult because searches had to be carried out, but I do know for sure -- I know that somebody sent us some helmets on this convoy, and then we returned them. I don't know whether it was some kind of like a French Battalion at the airport or something, so they should go back to them. But the convoys proceeded, and I don't think there were any problems at any time for a convoy carrying humanitarian aid to pass through Ilidza, Rajlovac, Ilijas. But if there was military equipment on the convoy, then there were problems and it was not approved. But humanitarian aid, food, medicines and so on, it passed through, there were no problems. The only thing that had to be done was to conduct a search to ascertain whether the cargo really was as it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir -- sorry. And do you know, sir, if there were ever any illegal trade that was being conducted with the humanitarian convoys during the period of 1992 through 1995, through the places that you've identified? Specifically, I think you said Sarajevo, Kiseljak, Ilidza, and then you mentioned a street, and I didn't get the correct spelling of that street, but I think it's Kasindolska, but we can talk about that later. Do you know if -- go ahead, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Kasindolska Street was the street leading from Ilidza to Sarajevo. It's a small street. Well, it's not important at all for this. But let me tell you, what can one suspect if, in a convoy with Red Cross insignia and flags, you find weapons and military equipment? Of course, this was illegal trafficking, smuggling. This may have been used by some NOGs, and in parallel some other people used it, but it is true there were such occasions. I received intelligence from our people, and we also did some intercepts. They were listening in to our conversations. We listened in to them. But I'm sure that some people tried to smuggle weapons and military equipment into Sarajevo, and of course then there would be counter-favours asked. That was there, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And, sir, just so that I'm clear, you weren't involved in investigating or doing any work with respect to that, or were you? That wasn't your task, was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not me specifically. I simply received intelligence about that, but I specifically did not do that. I recall that the military police squad from Ilidza searched a convoy there, and those helmets and weapons were found there. I personally did not take part in it, and this was not in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, my learned colleague Mr. Nikolic has raised in a note to me that I forgot to follow up on one thing. utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC

I have my own report, and I have certain documents that I have reviewed over the past few days in The Hague. And the Prosecution has also disclosed them over the past few days. I also have a case with documents in the witness room.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. About these new documents, I suppose they are the documents that the Prosecution disclosed on the 25th of July; last Friday, that is?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I also have some documents that the Prosecution disclosed in May, but I've only seen them recently in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: For the record again, please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Svetlana Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kindly tell us the date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sombor, Serbia, on the 14th November 1949.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please tell us something about your education.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I got my university degree from the University School for Philosophy in Belgrade. After that, I enrolled in post-graduate studies and obtained a Master's degree in the University Belgrade Faculty of Geography. And I later obtained a doctoral degree in 1999. The topic of my dissertation was the natural movement of populations of Serbia, and my doctorate was in the field of demography. The subject was populations in Kosovo and Metohija, an ethnographic and ethnogeographic study.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I work as a professor at the School of Geography of the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since when have you held this position?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your job, which subjects do you teach at the School of Geography at the Belgrade University?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The School of Geography has four chairs. One of them is demography. I teach at the chair of demography. I teach introduction into demography, statistics of population, and ethno-demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kindly tell us about your experience in the field of demography.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My entire career is directly linked to the study of population and demography. I got my first job in 1974 at the Republic Institute for Statistics in Serbia, and that was my first workplace. I remained there, dealing with statistics, until 1992. My career in statistics, I finished in the position of chief in the Department for Statistics of Population. It covers all the services that are in direct contact with the population, services for natural movements of populations, vital statistics, that is, censor statistics and migration statistics. While I worked at the Republic Institute for statistics, I was directly involved in creating all the methodologies used by these services but particularly the methodology of census. I participated indirectly in the census of 1971, namely, in the processing of data, not in creating methodology or implementation of census. In the 1981 and 1991 censuses, I was one of the members of what was then an inter-public group for the implementation of the methodology of the census and the processing of data, creation of tables, and displaying final results of the census. By virtue of my job, I led the 1991 census in Serbia. From 1991 onwards, that is, until 1999, I worked at the Institute for Humanities at the Centre of Demographic Research. The scope of my work in that institute meant that I took part in a number of research projects realised by this institute, and I personally led two research projects. One of them related to the population of Yugoslavia, according to the 1991 census, and another one to the agrarian population of Yugoslavia. In 1999, I moved to the Geography School of the University of Belgrade, and for a while I was head of the Department for Geography, and I was also deputy dean. I continued to work at the geographic school of the University of Belgrade, and I participated in a number of projects implemented by the School of Geography or other institutions such as the Academy of Science. I also took part in the implementation of research projects of the European Centre for Peace and Development of the United Nations. To date, I have published over 60 scientific and research papers that were published at the national level or at the international level.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are there any other projects that you were involved in, apart from these?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Projects of the European Centre for Peace and Development, projects of our Academy of Science.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Have you ever before testified as a demographic expert before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I testified in three cases; in the Galic case, and my evidence had to do with Sarajevo and the siege of Sarajevo; I testified in the Simic et al case, relating to Samac and Odzak; and in a case that was related to Srebrenica, but I can't remember the name of the client. I can only remember the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was it Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Blagojevic et al.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In relation to all these cases, you made your own expert report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you would be so kind to tell us something about demography. What kind of science is that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a very complex question, but I'll try to make it simple. Demography is a science that studies population, but it is only one of the sciences dealing with population, and it has its own particular aspects in studying certain phenomena related to population. It studies the demographic development of population, interrelations, causes and consequences of various trends that affect the demographic development. To put it very narrowly, "demographic development" implies studying two main components that affect increases and decreases of population and changes in its quantity or quality. So it studies natural movements of population, which again implies studying births, deaths, natality, reproductive capacities. And another component is the movement of population across territory; that is to say, migratory movements, such as emigration, immigration, silent migrations, et cetera. Demography is closely linked to other associated sciences, and it uses the methods and achievements of those related sciences, just as, in turn, it makes its own achievements and methods available to other related sciences. In that sense, demography is a multidisciplinary science. Within the framework of demography, there is a series of disciplines that focus on specific phenomena, such as economic demography, ethno-demography, medical demography, historical demography, et cetera. Certain authors characterize demography as the younger sister of statistics. To put it more precisely, it's -- all this discipline is the statistics of population. This speaks of the close relationship between statistics of the population with demography as a science. Very often, the scientific achievements and scope of demography, the level of development of demography, depend on the development of statistics of population; that is to say, to what extent statistics are able to provide reliable information and long-time series, that's very important, based on which demographic calculations and conclusions may be made. Looking at it that way, if you have good statistics of population, demography is able to study the development of population in the past, to provide its scientific evaluation of the development of population in the present, along with related problems, but also to forecast future developments of population. That would be the briefest answer I am capable of.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and explain to us what is necessary to do in order to be able to carry out reliable demographic analyses of a phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to do any kind of reliable demographic analysis, of course you have to have some demographic -- some knowledge of demography and statistics, and also you have to be familiar with the methods applied with demography and statistics. And it also helps if you're familiar with other scientific methods, but the key element for doing reliable demographic analysis is to have reliable statistical data. Only reliable statistical sources of statistical data make it possible to reach objectives and scientific conclusions about any phenomenon in demography that you're looking at at any given time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: For this case, you did an expert report entitled: "The Missing and Dead in Connection with Srebrenica," the 2005 report, and the number is 39 -- 3D 398. Could you please tell us, what was your task? What was the task that you had in front of you when you did this report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was my task to study all the reports done by Prosecution experts that have to do with Srebrenica, to study and analyse all the sources that were used by Prosecution experts in drafting their reports, to study and analyse all the available sources of data that I can access, to write a report in which I would also then talk about my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you were preparing this report, as you've just told us, you went through all the expert reports produced by Prosecution experts?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the reports that I knew of and that were accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your opinion of the report drafted in 2005 by Mr. Helge Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the reports drafted by Mr. Brunborg and his associates are based on results using methodologically inconsistent sources that abound in errors. Depending on the sources, the error range is between 30 to 100 per cent. Furthermore, the Prosecution experts modify the standards, statistical and demography methods, in such a way that they adapt them to their own needs so that they could get their own results. That is why the reports proffered by the Prosecution experts cannot be considered as scientifically sound, because they do not comply with any of the principles. They don't even meet the minimum requirements that are necessary for scientific research. It is my personal opinion that the reports filed by Prosecution experts create a great deal of confusion in the effort to get an objective perception of the events, and as such they cannot contribute to an objective analysis and study and an attempt to get at the phenomena and events they deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the report filed by Mr. Brunborg from 2005?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about that report, but also about the report that was drafted by Dr. Brunborg in 2000, the report that Dr. Brunborg wrote in 2003; and I'm also talking about two articles or papers that Dr. Brunborg published. I received them here. They're also sort of reports, so they were published in 2001, one in the Statistical Bulletin of the United Nations, and the second one, which is entitled: "The Genocide Count," I can't now see where it was published, but let me --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now I will start asking you questions about the basis for the findings that you started talking about. Can you please tell us something about the sources of the data used? What sources were used, how many were used by the Prosecution, by Mr. Brunborg in doing the report and getting to the findings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking about the data sources that could lead to a better understanding of the events in Srebrenica, well, I don't know of any, but Dr. Brunborg and his associates use four, or in the last report they mention six sources. The sources are the records of missing persons kept by the International Committee of the Red Cross, the records of the Physicians for Human Rights, the 1991 census, the electoral roles for 1997-1998 and 2008. The latter was used in the last report, and in the last report there is also the database on displaced persons, and yet another source, data on exhumed and identified bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber how many sources did you use in producing your expert report that was filed by the Defence teams to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I used all the reports that were used by the Prosecution experts - rather sources rather than reports - and all the sources that I have been able to find in the Demographic Unit of the Prosecution and all the documents that the Prosecution has disclosed to the Defence that I have obtained from the Defence, as well as sources that I obtained myself and that I felt might be relevant in relation to Srebrenica, such as the Bulletin of Displaced Persons published by a Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all those reports that were not drafted by demographers, but that could contain some data that might be used to orient oneself, such as, for instance, the report by Mr. Marin. I'm not sure now, but I think that I used 22 reports. I'm not sure about the number, but I can check. Twenty-two sources, rather. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would like to ask you now: When you did your analysis, did you notice any deficiency in the way in which sources were used by the Prosecution in order to obtain their results and to do the lists of missing persons in Srebrenica in 1995, or the list of missing persons in 2005?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that, but perhaps I was not clear enough. All the sources have this major deficiency, because they're all methodologically inconsistent and they contain a huge number of errors. As I already indicated, the error range is between 30 and 100 per cent. But Prosecution experts also note the key deficiencies in their reports, and I fully agree with them. For instance, in their reports -- or, rather, one of the papers published, Dr. Brunborg highlights, as the key problems for the sources that he has used, he indicates the problem of scope, of coverage. And then there is the accuracy of the data in the source. And the third key problem noted by him is lack of information. All those things indicate that the sources of data are of low or limited quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to tell us, since you've already mentioned all the sources that both you and the Prosecution used, to tell us something about the Red Cross list, as one of the sources for the data, the ICRC list, their missing persons list.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, before I go on to say something about those two key basic sources, I would like to note that I don't know how many sources there are, and that at one point I tried to learn something about at least those sources that are in the possession of the Prosecution. But I always had to instruct the Prosecution and be quite specific about what sources I was looking for. I am saying this because I want to limit myself in this way to say that perhaps there are other sources in the possession of the Prosecution or someplace else that I have been unable to consult. So the sources that I list are the sources that I was able to see in the Prosecution, but I did not have an overview of all the sources and then to say, "I want this, this and that," but I always had to name the source that I was looking for. In order to be able to do that, I had to study their reports and look for reference there. I listened to their evidence, and then I was able to learn that there were some other sources of data available. You asked me to comment on the ICRC as a source and also the Physicians for Human Rights list as a source. Dr. Brunborg notes that these are the best sources that he used, and I would like to note that these are the only sources in existence. I wouldn't go as far as to say that they are the best, because you can't really compare them to any other sources that would apply the same methodology and collect data in the same manner. It is general knowledge that the International Red Cross is a humanitarian organisation, and in this case it collected data about missing persons, with the objective of making it possible for the relatives to find their next of kin. The methodology applied by the ICRC in collecting the data is diametrically opposed to the manner in which statistical data are gathered.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what is it, this methodology?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll explain that, but the Red Cross is not a statistical organisation and it was not bound by this methodology. The methodology used by the ICRC to collect data was based on questionnaires containing a certain number of questions, and the questionnaires were filled in by people who came to report that their family members or their acquaintances were missing. They filled them in either personally or through the mediation of somebody else. The ICRC then put some of those data into the computer, and every person was given a numerical designation. This was probably done in order to be able to process the data more easily, because the ICRC reviewed the data three -- two or three times. But as I said, it was not the task of the ICRC to collect, correct, put data in the tables, in the same way in which it is done by the statistics. The ICRC published the data, and for a time you could even access the data on the internet. Unlike the ICRC -- or, rather, let me say this: ICRC worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991 until the end of the war, 1996, in other words, but it is still active in those areas and it is now doing other things. Unlike the ICRC, the Physicians for Human Rights did not cover the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina in its operations, but it focused exclusively on Eastern Bosnia. When I say "Eastern Bosnia," I actually mean just part of Eastern Bosnia. And it has some data for Sarajevo that it collected. And as we all know, Sarajevo is not Eastern Bosnia. The questionnaire that was used by the Physicians for Human Rights to collect their data, it has more than 20 pages. It is very, very complicated. It includes some medical information and some other kinds of expertise that's required. I don't know what the procedure is, whether people came to their offices to report or whether their researchers went out in the field, where they heard about some cases of missing persons, but PHR collected information about the deceased persons in order to put together an antemortem database. As far as I know, the revision of the data collected by the PHR was done once. This is what Dr. Brunborg notes; it was done in 1999, but I don't know whether the data gathered by the PHR has ever been made public anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. Now that we're talking about the PHR or the database of the Physicians for Human Rights, could you please tell us what area you're talking about? Is it the Srebrenica area or some other area?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the area for which there are data. We have data for parts of Eastern Bosnia, but it mostly deals with Srebrenica or, rather, the area of Tuzla and its environs. There is -- there are some data for Sarajevo, and for the most part data were collected in 1996. I don't know that off the top of my head, but we can look at the report. They started gathering information from 1991, but the data for years that followed, 1992, 1993, varies greatly, a thousand, two thousand, but the largest number is for 1996. What I'm telling you now is based on Dr. Brunborg's report and what I have been able to look at in the OTP Demographic Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about the quality of the sources, when you talked about both the ICRC and the PHR. Could we wrap up this topic with the following question: What is the quality of those sources, according to Dr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to Dr. Brunborg, their quality is not good, but these are good sources. Well, this perhaps is a caricature, but if you want me to, I can find the quote in his report, because Dr. Brunborg says that in each of the two have their strengths and weaknesses. I haven't been able to notice any advantages, but among the drawbacks he lists a lot of empty fields, data that doesn't exist, a large number of errors in the data that was in, especially when it comes to first name, last name, date of birth and so on. But this might be characterized as an advantage, although I don't see it as such. He says when you put together the two sources, then you get a source where the two corroborate each other. This doesn't sound logical to me, especially in light of the number of errors. I can't see how the two reports corroborate each other. And I would also like to draw your attention to this fact: Both in statistical and in demographic terms, this is quite important. Technically speaking, those two sources put together data that concerns different units of observation. The Red Cross collects information about the missing persons, and at one point they're not characterized in any other way. These people are listed as missing, whereas the PHR collects information about the dead in order to put together an antemortem database.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about ICRC lists as one of the sources for your report, did you have occasion to gain insight into the raw material, these questionnaires handed out by the ICRC, where all the necessary information is filled in?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have access to that. I invested a lot of effort to get to the raw material. Generally speaking, raw material is very important for statisticians. However, I am not an institution myself and I was never able to get access to the raw material. As far as I'm aware, not even the Prosecution has the raw material, I mean, those questionnaires. I don't know whether they ever attempted to get them from the ICRC, but I believe it would be extremely important to have them and that, at the very initial stage, a major error was made precisely because we are not in possession of the raw material that would give us a great number of characteristics that could have, at a later stage, given us a substantially different qualitative evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What are these characteristics in questionnaires? I want the Trial Chamber to understand what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The ICRC collects information about their first name, last name, father's name, date and place of birth, and date and place of disappearance, ethnicity and the status of persons who went missing. When I say "status," it means whether the person was a soldier or a civilian. You even have information about their rank, their unit, their marital status, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would this raw material facilitate more accurate identification of people who were targeted by both reports?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I won't talk about accurate identification, because it is a fact that many errors were made in many rubrics concerning many characteristics, but I think it would have been very important to a professional demographer, statistician, to see that there are certain characteristics, such as place of permanent residence, which in our case is very important in order to define the area we are dealing with, and it would have been very important, at the very beginning of the Srebrenica project, to be able to establish that these were not solely civilians, or non-combatants as Dr. Brunborg names them, that a great number of soldiers are involved. I think that qualitatively, it would have given us perhaps a completely different view of the situation. Whether it would quantitatively change the findings, I don't know, because I haven't seen the raw material. However, when a professional statistician sees a questionnaire, he can precisely define the unit and the area he wants to study, and there is a very precise standard procedure in statistics as to how to gather information, how to evaluate their quality, how to improve their quality. And using that procedure, perhaps Dr. Brunborg would have arrived at a smaller number of persons. That, I don't know, but I have no doubt that the quality of information would have been significantly better. Maybe the resulting number of persons would have been even higher. In any case, I emphasise the quality would have been better, and it would have been important.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How would that have affected the quality of the list of the missing persons for 2000 and 2005?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I believe this piece of information, the place of permanent residence, is very important, because the ICRC gathered that information. It was not officially published. I cannot of its quality. But it would have been very important, because it precisely defines the area that needs to be analysed. And, generally speaking, in all reports there is this horrendous problem of defining what is Srebrenica. In different situations, it is viewed differently. I was about to say it was defined differently, but there is no definition. It is viewed very differently. It could be 13 municipalities, 15 municipalities, or anything else. If we had this piece of information, we would have qualitatively different information, or at least we would have had a sample of permanent residence. Another important thing, it would have dispelled certain illusions about the status of missing and dead persons resulting from the events in Srebrenica in 1995. It is a fact that this list does not include only non-combatants, but combatants as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Kindly tell us, why is the 1991 Bosnia and Herzegovina census and the voters' lists for 1997-1998 important as a source of statistical data?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was important to the Prosecution experts for two main reasons. The census was important to them in order to prove that the persons recorded in their list are not fictitious, nonexistent persons; that they were real persons who existed in reality because they were recorded in the voters' lists for 1997 -- in the 1991 census, sorry. Voters' lists, as a source of information, had the purpose to prove that there are no survivors included in the Prosecution's lists of dead, but I have to explain this more elaborately. The method used by Prosecution experts is the method of matching. What does "matching" mean? The method of matching means that using a proper statistical procedure, you can, from two or more sources, identify a certain statistical unit, that is, a person in this case, in more than one source. How can you identify it? You identify it by establishing an identification key. The identification key represents certain characteristics based on which you can, with a great degree of reliability, claim that the person from one list has been identified in a second, third, or fifth list. When the key is numeric, it's not a problem, and all of us in our daily lives use the method of matching. Everybody who has a bank card falls in one database. They form one group, and the banks have their database. In order to collect money from an ATM, you have to put your card in, of course, but you have to also provide a key, that is, a sequence of four or more numbers. If you do not identify yourself properly by this numeric key, there is no matching and you can't collect the money. Since in some of these censuses we don't have numeric keys, since in some of these sources we don't have keys, we have them in the census because everybody has their own unique identification number, but we don't have them in the ICRC lists. Then the Prosecution experts had to choose an identification key for matching. This key should meet the elementary requirements for reliability of the resulting finding. Prosecution experts have 71 keys. Using 71 keys, if you ask me, you can match anything you please, and the fact that Prosecution witnesses have 71 keys would not be such a great problem, although it's completely inappropriate, if the Prosecution experts had, in any one of their reports, cited the statistics of matching by individual keys. What does statistics of matching me mean? That means on the first criterion, name, father's name, date of birth, we found so many matches. Without the father's name, we matched 30 per cent. Without the date of birth, we matched 70 per cent. Why is this important? Because these statistics demonstrate the combinatorics based on which we can make a judgement on which information can be accepted as relatively reliable, as opposed to information that we should reject as completely unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have finished with this segment, I would like to go back to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was about to take a breath and -- well, by matching your list with information from the census, Dr. Brunborg identifies persons and says: "I claim that these persons do exist, and they were recorded in the census of 1991." Such matches amounted to 87 per cent, in Dr. Brunborg's report, on, I emphasise, 71 criteria. Why they arrived at 87 per cent, I really wasn't able to discover. On the other hand, by matching with voters' lists, if you ask me, this matching was not done using all criteria, because using all criteria you should be able to find a lot of matches. You have certain criteria that use only initials and a date of birth, plus/minus five. In the census of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have three Svetlana Radovanovics. According to this criterion, Dr. Brunborg would identify me as well, although I'm a resident of Serbia. So in my opinion, in order to identify survivors, in comparison with voters' lists, Dr. Brunborg did not use all this criteria. And not only did he fail to use all this criteria. I wouldn't know whether he used the first or the second or the first, second and third, because it's impossible to determine. Instead, Dr. Brunborg narrowed down the area within which he is making the matches, seeking matches. What does "narrowing down" mean? When he identifies a list of survivors -- or, rather, when he looks for survivors in the census, compared to his list, then the survivors could be anyone in Eastern Bosnia, and there could be 400.000 of them. I don't know exactly the population of Eastern Bosnia. When he seeks to identify survivors, he doesn't identify them in all Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would have been normal, because the voters who had fled from any locality in 1991 had the right to vote in other municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They even had the right to vote from abroad. So people living in Srebrenica, whatever that means, whether it's just Srebrenica municipality or the surrounding five municipalities, did not have to register for voting only there. So Dr. Brunborg is not looking for voters from all over Bosnia. He is not even looking for them in Eastern Bosnia. He's looking for them in certain frameworks that he defines as Srebrenica. What does that mean? That means that he completely overlooked a significant number of people. I made a test only on Srebrenica municipality. From the Srebrenica municipality, I was able to find over 12.000 people who originally come from Srebrenica and registered for voting in Tuzla, Jajce, Sarajevo, and other municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Out of those, one-third are men of 18. Within the number of voters who come from Srebrenica originally, but registered to vote abroad, I found 2.000. So a significant portion of the population of Srebrenica, and I'm talking only about men because I took into account only men, were not even taken into account when trying to find matches, and I think that is very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In order to establish that, did you spend some time working on the material available at the Demographic Unit of the OTP here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent seven days working with this material in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor, I have two corrections for the transcript. On page 86, lines 6 and 7, you said that according to the matching methods, using 71 keys, possible matching were 71 to how many per cent?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I said if you have 71 keys for matching, you can match anything. Now, what's the problem with this? If you don't have complete identification based on which I can assert with full certainty that Svetlana, daughter of Dragan Radovanovic, was born on 18 November 1949, when I say "completely reliably," that's with a great degree of reliability, that such a person was identified also in another source of information, then the problem is: How can you decide that somebody has initials or just the last and first name without father's name, or just last and first name and the year of birth? How do you know that this is indeed the same person? If you have information about the place of birth that may or may not be true, and you have no information about permanent residency, then you are forced to use something that Dr. Brunborg qualifies as the visual method, which of course exists as such, but in statistics the visual method is not so important as it may be in some other sciences. I'm not saying this method does not exist. In the logical control of certain information in the questionnaire, you use the visual method. I can see that this is the person that graduated from primary school and cites his occupation as university professor. Of course, looking at these two piece of information, I see something is wrong, and then I proceed to look at the whole questionnaire to show me where the mistake is, whether it's with the degree of education or with the current occupation. That's the kind of visual methods that statisticians use. But any visual method, including this one, opens the door to subjective decisions, and I think -- in fact, I don't think, Prosecution experts say that thousands upon thousands of cases were determined using the visual method. I'm not saying that all of these thousands relate only to Srebrenica, but I'm saying that method is used here in many reports, and that's why I think -- in fact, I don't think, it simply isn't reliable because it may be subjective.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have completed one topic, and perhaps this could be a good moment to adjourn until tomorrow. Thank you, Professor Radovanovic. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you think you need, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I expect, Your Honour, certainly 45 minutes, perhaps even an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had requested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought it was an hour and a half, but I'll look into that. I think in total, we may have put "four hours," because each team were going to take a half an hour and a half, but I'll look into that. I don't believe that I personally was going to ask for four hours, but I'll look into it. It won't be four hours. It will be closer to an hour or an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll see where we've got to, but it looks like everything's going to be pretty comprehensibly covered before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Soljan, what's your expected duration of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: At this time, I believe two hours, as we had indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So tomorrow we'll have the extended sitting. In other words, we'll finish at 3.30. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
